title: Is Britain really a democracy? These days I’m not so sure
snippet: The Starmer Government's EU reset suggests that Brexit failed to engender a sense of democratic responsibility among the establishment class.

Log in or Subscribe Copy link X Icon twitter Facebook Icon facebook WhatsApp Icon whatsapp email Add us as preferred source Credit: Andy Rain/Shutterstock Robert Tombs Published 19 April 2026 8:00am BST Much is badly wrong in many of what were once confidently called “mature democracies”. Their malaise has common features, but each country has its own particular symptoms.Britain’s now include an assault on democratic legitimacy – not a frontal assault, but a contemptuous determination to ignore public wishes and even to subvert a legally expressed democratic decision. Ignoring public sentiment is most evident in the whole establishment attitude to mass immigration and its consequences. Subverting a democratic decision is blatant in the present Government’s “reset” with the European Union.After the referendum vote, as all readers will recall, Remainers campaigned for a second referendum. That at least was open and honest. But they were decisively defeated again in the 2019 general election, and their campaign fell apart. Their tactic now is to avoid a popular vote and even to evade parliamentary scrutiny by using so-called “Henry VIII” powers to return the UK to the EU’s regulatory orbit. The effect will be to nullify the 2016 referendum without a public debate or consultation. The Government’s EU rest is a subversion of a democratic decision Credit: James Veysey/Shutterstock This raises a wider question in my mind: do we really live in a democracy? Our rulers seem to be scrambling to revert to a pre-democratic age. I keep thinking of the so-called Great Reform Act of 1832. The weight of public opinion, often violently expressed, forced Parliament to accept constitutional reform as a first step towards a transformation of the state and society. But those in power made sure it had the opposite effect. Their “reform” deliberately made the system less democratic, disfranchising working-class voters, explicitly denying women a vote, and buttressing the dominance of the propertied elite.As in the case of Brexit, the intention was to stifle a popular initiative. This was not done by reactionary Tories but by arrogantly progressive Whigs, convinced of their superior right to rule. Robert Lowe, a leading Liberal of a later generation, speaking for “every cultivated Englishman”, vehemently opposed “a democratic basis” for government as it would affect “all your other institutions”.Lowe was once ridiculed by progressives, but now his view coincides with theirs. Our institutions, and government itself, are to be insulated from “populism”, which the philosopher John Gray has aptly defined as “a term liberals use to describe the political blow back against the social disruption that their policies have created”.Anti-democratic reflexA few months ago, I took part in an international conference on “Populism” at the European Parliament, where I was in a minority of one. I was wryly amused to observe that indignation towards populism was particularly heated when what the populists were saying was true. How dare they tell people that Euro-MPs have chauffeur-driven cars!As for the British Left, its anti-democratic reflex goes back at least to its repeated inability to win over the public during the Thatcher era. The clearest sign was a change of mind over what became the European Union, to which Labour had traditionally been hostile, seeing it as an undemocratic capitalist organisation.In 1988, Jacques Delors, president of the European Commission, won them over by promising European legislation to counter Thatcherism. They saw that “Europe” could provide Left-wing groups with the means of importing laws that the benighted British public would not vote for. This seems to remain their hope. Margaret Thatcher supported economic integration, but vehemently deepening political union within the EU Credit: Christophe Simon/AFP As Tony Blair realised, Labour could only win elections by pretending to be something different.
